messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  (none)

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  (none)

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

She remembers the weight of the evening—how the courthouse hallways had emptied, how her own footsteps echoed off the tile as she gathered her coat near the side exit. It was a shortcut she had taken for thirty years, a path that saved her seven minutes of walking around the block. The man came from behind the stairwell door, and before she could register his face, his arm was around her throat, and her briefcase hit the floor. He did not take her wallet. He said things she has never repeated. The whole thing lasted perhaps ninety seconds, but those seconds rewired something fundamental. She was seventy-six years old, a public defender who had argued felony cases for four decades, and she had never once felt small in a hallway until that night.

In the months that followed, the world became a place of hidden threats. She began to watch people—really watch them—in a way she never had before. On the street, in the grocery store, even in the courthouse lobby, her eyes would scan for the subtle signs: a hand in a pocket, a person standing too still, someone who angled their body toward her rather than past her. She had always been observant; it was part of what made her a good lawyer. But this was different. This was a vigilance that never switched off. She would catch herself staring at a man in the elevator until he looked uncomfortable, and she would know she was doing it, and she would not stop.

Her husband noticed first. He would touch her shoulder to get her attention, and she would flinch—a sharp, full-body startle that embarrassed them both. The sound of a car backfiring on their quiet street would send her heart into her throat for a full ten minutes. She started to avoid the side exit at work, then the parking garage, then the walk from the garage to the building. Her paralegal began meeting her at the front door with a coffee, walking her in. She told herself it was practical. She told herself she was being smart.

But the checking became a habit she could not break. Every time she walked anywhere—from her car to the courthouse, from the courthouse to the bus stop, from the kitchen to the bedroom at night—she would glance behind her. Sometimes twice. Sometimes she would stop and turn fully, scanning the empty corridor or sidewalk, and she knew how strange it looked, and she did it anyway. She had come to believe that if she stopped checking, she would be caught off guard again. That the only reason she had survived the first time was luck, and luck was not a strategy.

She is still working, still going to court, still cross-examining witnesses with the same sharp precision. But she arrives early now, and she leaves late, and she always asks a colleague to walk her to her car. Her husband has offered to drive her, but she refuses. She tells him it is not necessary. What she does not tell him is that she does not want him to see how often she looks behind her, how she cannot help it, how her body responds to a sudden noise before her mind can catch up. She came to therapy because her granddaughter asked her why she seemed scared all the time. She did not have an answer. She is hoping to find one.
